segments.text: Naungan means shelter. It is cash that reaches families before a flood, a heatwave or a cyclone.
Today, aid agencies cannot see each other's lists. Some families are paid twice, others are missed, and the money arrives after the water.
When the World Food Programme paid families days before the 2020 Jamuna flood peaked, they were 36 percent less likely to go a day without eating.
Naungan coordinates without sharing. Agencies compare lists by private set intersection, and only anonymous commitments go on-chain.
Two independent forecasts must agree before claims open, and each family claims from its phone with a zero-knowledge proof: paid once, and nobody can tell who was paid.
Blockchains already move aid. What is new: no list leaves an agency, money moves before the disaster, and anyone can verify every payout.
10 live programs in 6 countries, each on the trigger the local Red Cross or Red Crescent society published.
Replayed over thirty years, the Aceh trigger would have paid 7 times, most recently on 23 Nov 2025, and held back 8 rain-only alarms.
And anyone can check any river on Earth. Here is Sylhet, in Bangladesh.
The page finds the main river, its flood level, and how often a program there would have paid.
The public dashboard is rebuilt from chain events, in your browser. No household is ever named.
The oracles post their forecasts with evidence, and anyone can recompute a report in their own browser.
Official GDACS alerts and the Red Cross plan for the area sit beside the trigger.
In plain words: Claude explains the trigger in the family's language, shown only if every number matches the on-chain facts.
Running costs are measured from real transactions: about half a cent for a family's claim on Base.
Families rate the aid with a second zero-knowledge proof: one rating per family, never linked to its payment.
Verify every payout: this browser fetches each claim transaction and checks its zero-knowledge proof again.
Auditors sign the result on the Ethereum Attestation Service, so donors count independent checks instead of trusting us.
Each program's payouts are also a hypercert, on Hypercerts' own contract, split among the donors who paid for them.
Anyone can re-check the certificate on Hypercerts' four counts, then sign the evaluation on-chain.
This is the family's claim app. It works offline, reads aloud, and speaks seven languages.
Why this money? The trigger, explained from public facts only. Nothing about the family is sent.
Tapping Claim proves the family is enrolled without saying who it is. One US dollar lands in about twelve seconds, and judges can try this very card.
Families with a phone register themselves. The phone keeps its secret and shows only an anonymous registration code, with the amount in local money.
The agency pastes the codes it collected and enrolls them in one transaction, from its own wallet.
Two agencies check their lists against each other without either seeing the other's names. The list never leaves this computer.
Any agency can launch a program from a published Early Action Protocol: the trigger, the place, the people within reach and the budget.
A printable poster, in English or the local language, invites households to register with a QR code.
And partners embed a live card of any program on their own site.
Donors see where every gift went, checked against the contract's own record.
And they claim their fraction of each impact certificate, to keep, give, or offer to a retroactive funder.
Everything is open data in the formats aid already reads: IATI, HXL, GeoJSON, and bilingual CAP alerts that national warning systems can relay.
The contract has no owner, so nobody can change the rules after donors give.
It is rehearsed on a fork of Base mainnet with Circle's real USDC, and checked by more than two hundred and forty automated tests.
Try it at naungan dot vercel dot app.
